chief_complaint: Difficulty in walking, starting just over 2 years prior to presentation.
history_of_present_illness: The illness started suddenly, with the boy first noticing his legs felt heavy and began to tremble while walking home from school, causing difficulty in walking and a tendency to fall. Since that day, he has been unable to stand or walk unaided, now standing on his toes and dragging his legs around with the aid of a stick. He denies any history of fever, pain, sensory, bladder or bowel symptoms or disease progression. The onset was acute and the course has been non-progressive over 2 years.
exposure_and_epidemiology: He lives in a village in northern Tanzania, a rural area with limited agricultural suitability where the main staple food crop is cassava. His diet for the 2 months before the illness was almost exclusively cassava. He has three other siblings, one of whom is similarly affected. Identical cases had occurred in his own and neighbouring villages at around the same time.
physical_exam: He is well nourished. General examination is unremarkable. On neurological examination, he is fully orientated and higher mental function appear normal. Cranial nerves are normal but bilateral optic pallor was noted on fundoscopy. Limbs reveal signs of spastic paraparesis with flexion contractures at both ankles and knees. Power in the legs is graded 3 to 4 out of 5, with the knee extensors and foot dorsiflexors involved to the greatest extent. There is bilateral hypertonia, hyperreflexia and sustained ankle clonus with extensor plantar responses. The arms are normal apart from generalized hyperreflexia. There is no impairment or loss of sensation. A lumbar lordosis with thoracic kyphoscoliosis is noticeable only on standing.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood glucose and creatinine are normal. Urine analysis is normal. Microscopy of urine and stool specimens does not show any ova of Schistosoma species. HIV serology and VDRL are negative. Lumbar puncture is normal. Radiographs of the chest and thoracolumbar spine are normal.
differential_diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses considered in Africa include spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease), transverse myelitis, spinal cord infections such as schistosomiasis and tuberculous myelitis, spinal malignancy (mainly metastases), and tropical nutritional myeloneuropathies. Spinal tuberculosis, spinal cord infection, or spinal malignancy are considered very unlikely due to three key features: isolated involvement of motor neurons without sensory or bladder involvement, absence of back pain, and acute onset with no progression over 2 years. Among tropical myeloneuropathies, lathyrism is ruled out as it occurs exclusively in Ethiopia, pointing towards konzo.
management_and_clinical_course: There is no cure for patients with konzo as it results in permanent spastic paraparesis. Management is directed at support, symptomatic improvement, and disease prevention. The majority of patients can walk with the aid of a stick or crutches, and some may benefit from a wheelchair. Muscle relaxants have limited effectiveness due to spasticity severity and high cost. Surgical treatment, such as Achilles tendon lengthening operations, has been useful in improving mobilization for selected patients. This patient should be assessed for surgery due to the severity of his contractures. At follow-up examination at 6 and 12 months, the findings were unchanged, with a permanent spastic paraparesis. The patient was not referred for surgery due to a lack of resources and the extent of the epidemic. He uses one stick with very restricted mobility and works as a shoe repairer in his village.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is Konzo, a distinct form of tropical spastic paraparesis. This condition is attributed to chronic high dietary exposure to cyanogenic glycosides from insufficiently processed cassava tubers. The diagnosis is supported by the symmetrical spastic paraparesis without sensory or genitourinary involvement, abrupt onset in less than 1 week with a non-progressive course over 2 years, its occurrence in a cassava-growing area with other similar cases, and the exclusion of other causes through comprehensive investigations.

images.caption: A 14-year-old boy from rural Tanzania with spastic paraparesis. His illness started about 2 years earlier and had an acute onset. Several other people are also affected in his own and neighbouring villages.
